Emotion Control.short_definition: Rewarding the feelings a person is allowed to show and punishing or shaming the rest, until they perform emotions instead of reporting them.
Emotion Control.core_meaning: Rewarding the feelings a person is allowed to show and punishing or shaming the rest, until they perform emotions instead of reporting them.
Emotion Control.expanded_definition: Emotion control is a pattern in which a household, relationship or group sets which feelings may be shown and enforces it through reactions that differ by feeling. Cheerfulness and gratitude get warmth. Anger, sadness or doubt get coldness, shame or a lecture. Some versions also demand that feelings be confessed on request. One tense reaction to one outburst means little. Weight comes from repetition: the same feelings are penalized every time, whatever the situation, and the person starts editing themselves before anyone has reacted.
Emotion Control.plain_language_summary: Some of your feelings are welcome and others cost you something, so you learn to show only the welcome ones, even at home.
Emotion Control.why_this_matters: When only some feelings are safe to show, you stop reporting the rest and may eventually stop noticing them. What is left of your emotional life is the part that was permitted.
what_it_is: Approval handed out for certain feelings (cheerfulness, gratitude, calm) and withdrawn for others (anger, grief, fear, doubt).
Demands for positivity in the middle of a real problem, such as being told to smile or be thankful when something has gone wrong.
Requests to confess how you feel, followed by that confession being kept and used later as proof of a flaw.
Penalties out of scale with the feeling: days of silence, a long lecture, or mockery after a mild complaint.
Found in couples, families, workplaces with mandatory enthusiasm, and tightly run groups.
what_it_sounds_like: Smile. Nobody wants to see that face at dinner.
You have so much to be grateful for. Why are you crying?
Go on, tell me how you really feel. (Later:) So you admit you resent me.
Don't you dare raise your voice in this house.
We don't do negativity here.
I'll talk to you when you're in a better mood.
Look how lovely you are when you're not complaining.
what_it_is_not: A household or workplace with norms about how feelings get expressed, such as no shouting at the table. Cultures differ widely, and a difference in emotional style is not a tactic.
A norm that falls evenly on everyone in the room, including the person who set it, instead of landing on one person as a penalty for particular feelings.
Someone asking for a calmer tone in the middle of a heated argument, then coming back to hear you out.
A person who finds sadness or anger hard to be near, says so, and does not punish you for having it.
A job that asks for steady composure with customers while leaving room to be human elsewhere.
One kind attempt to cheer you up that you are free to turn down.
this_may_be_it_when: The same feeling gets a cold, shaming or angry response on many different days, whatever the topic.
Your good moods are noticed and praised while your low ones are called a phase, a mood or an act.
You rehearse a cheerful face before walking in the door.
A feeling you admitted when asked is quoted back at you in a later argument.
The reaction to a mild feeling is far bigger than the feeling was.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The other person hides anger and tears too, and the rule applies to everyone equally.
Disagreement and upset are welcome as long as they come without contempt or shouting.
A request to pause comes with a promise to return, and they do.
You can name a person or place where the same feeling is received without a cost.
The sensitivity is about one subject, such as a recent death, and not about a whole range of feelings.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Someone raised in a home where feelings were never discussed may simply have no practice receiving them.
A tired or overloaded person can lack room for someone else's upset, which says little about whether the feeling is allowed to exist.
A culture or faith tradition may prize restraint, and the person holding that norm may apply it to themselves as well.
common_false_positives: A friend who says they cannot hear this right now and asks to talk tomorrow, then does.
A team lead who asks for a steady manner in front of clients.
A parent teaching a child not to hit when angry, while still letting the anger itself be spoken.
discernment_questions: Which feelings can I show here without a price, and which ones cost me something?
Do I act out feelings I do not have, and who am I protecting when I do?
Does the other person hide the same feelings, or is it only me who is expected to?
Can I remember a time I said I was sad or angry and was simply heard?
Is the reaction in proportion to what I said, or does it work to shut the feeling down?
less_concerning_if: The norms are stated openly, hold for everyone, and can be talked about.
Anger or sadness is met with a request for a different time or tone, not with withdrawn warmth.
You still have at least one place where you can show your full range.
more_concerning_if: Warmth, money or privileges rise and fall with whether you look cheerful.
Feelings you confessed are stored and brought back as evidence that you are difficult.
When someone asks what you feel, you find you no longer know.
pattern_over_time_signs: Your range narrows: fewer complaints, fewer tears, then fewer reports of delight as well.
You answer 'how are you' with 'fine', even to people who would listen.
You edit messages to remove anything that sounds negative before sending.
Friends say you seem flat, or that you used to be more expressive.
Emotion Control.repair_check: The next time you are visibly sad or angry is when it shows. Repair here shows up as the same warmth arriving whether or not you are cheerful. An apology for a harsh reaction, followed by the cold shoulder on your next low day, has not changed the rule.
Emotion Control.boundary_respect_check: Think about what it costs to say 'I'm not okay today' a week after asking for room to feel things. If the answer is nothing, the request landed. If the price is back, in sighs, silence or a lecture, it did not.
Emotion Control.psychological_mechanism: People adjust what they show in order to keep approval and avoid pain, and the adjustment can become automatic. When warmth reliably follows some feelings and withdrawal follows others, a person can learn to suppress the penalized ones before they surface. Being asked to confess feelings on demand can add a second pressure: anything admitted may be kept. Over time the habit can reach the feeling itself, not just its display.
Emotion Control.possible_impact_on_receiver: Accounts include numbness or flatness at home, not knowing what you feel when asked, rehearsing cheerful answers, and crying only when alone. Some report feeling fake in their own family, or noticing that relief at leaving the house was the only strong feeling left. Others are surprised at how quickly anger and grief came back once the penalty was gone.

response_options.soft_clarification: Name the pattern of reaction, not the person: 'When I say I'm sad, the room goes cold. I'd like to be able to say it and have you just listen.'
response_options.firm_boundary: State what you will and won't do tonight: 'I'm not going to pretend to be fine. I'm tired, and that's all I'm saying.'
response_options.disengagement: When a feeling is being ridiculed, take it out of the room for a while: a walk, a bath, a call to a friend who lets you have it.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell someone who has seen you in many moods what you have stopped saying at home. A counselor can help you test whether your range has narrowed.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Where cheerfulness is part of the job culture, keep your composure with clients, and find one manager or colleague one-to-one where you can say 'this week was hard' plainly.

Emotion Control.boundary_script: "I can be kind and calm with you, but I can't be cheerful on command. If I'm sad or angry, I want to say so once and have you hear it without a lecture."
Emotion Control.safety_note: Being punished for a feeling is pressure on your inner life, not a physical danger. It can change when the penalty for a feeling includes threats, intimidation when you show anger, or control of money or contact. Another sign is a mood being treated as proof you are unfit or unwell. If a reaction to a feeling ever frightens you, tell a friend, a doctor or a domestic abuse advocate what happens in the minutes after you speak.
misuse_warning: Calling every request for calm 'emotion control' can turn an ordinary ask to lower the volume into an accusation. The label fits when penalties fall repeatedly on particular feelings.
Using it to excuse your own outbursts, as if any limit on how you express anger were control, misreads it.
Emotion Control.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Nonverbal Dominance uses sighs, stares and eye rolls to unsettle or dismiss you in a single moment. Emotion control is the lasting rule about which feelings may appear at all, and a sigh or a stare may be one way it gets enforced. Ritualized Exhaustion drains your capacity through schedules and lost sleep, while emotion control leaves your energy alone and works on what you show.

Ritualized Exhaustion.short_definition: A relentless run of schedules, demands and lost sleep that keeps a person too depleted to think clearly, weigh options or push back.
Ritualized Exhaustion.core_meaning: A relentless run of schedules, demands and lost sleep that keeps a person too depleted to think clearly, weigh options or push back.
Ritualized Exhaustion.expanded_definition: Ritualized exhaustion is a sustained pattern of fixed routines, constant demands and cut-down sleep that leaves a person chronically worn out instead of briefly busy. It can appear in a household, a workplace, a caregiving arrangement or a tightly run group. A hard week or a launch crunch is not this. What sets it apart is a load with no end date, rest treated as laziness or failure, and a reduced ability to think and object that nobody acknowledges.
Ritualized Exhaustion.plain_language_summary: You are kept so busy and so short of sleep that you have nothing left for thinking, deciding or saying no.
Ritualized Exhaustion.why_this_matters: Depletion that runs for months narrows the ability to think, weigh options and push back, and once that is gone, noticing its absence gets harder too.
what_it_is: Fixed routines, such as early wake-ups, late-night tasks and set check-ins, that crowd out sleep, meals and time alone.
Demands that arrive as fast as the last one is finished, so catching up never happens.
Rest treated as a lapse: tiredness gets called weakness, poor attitude or lack of commitment.
An open-ended quality: nobody can say when the pace will ease.
Seen in households, caregiving, workplaces and tightly run groups where keeping the schedule is part of belonging.
what_it_sounds_like: You can sleep when the work is done.
If you were really committed, you wouldn't need eight hours.
Just one more thing before you go to bed.
Everyone else manages fine.
A message or task lands at 2 a.m. and a reply is expected within minutes.
A schedule with no free day, and a day off that gets filled at the last minute.
Being told you look tired, followed by another task.
what_it_is_not: A hard stretch with a real, disclosed end point, such as a launch, a new baby or a family crisis. A demanding period that ends is different from an open-ended schedule that never gives rest back.
Choosing a punishing schedule yourself because you love the project or are training for something.
Shift work, on-call duty or night nursing, where hours are tough but agreed, paid and followed by recovery.
A chaotic household or office where nobody is rested, including the person making the demands.
Insomnia, anxiety or a health condition wearing you down without anyone imposing a schedule.
Caring for a sick relative, where the demands come from the illness itself.
this_may_be_it_when: Nobody can give you a date or a condition for when the load will ease.
Requests for sleep or a day off are answered with doubt about your commitment.
The demands rise after you have shown signs of objecting.
Your errors and slowness get noted, but the hours behind them do not.
You notice you now agree to things you would have refused when rested.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The heavy period has a named end and you can see it coming.
The person setting the pace works the same hours and is exhausted too.
You can refuse a task and the refusal is accepted.
Time off is given back after a crunch.
You chose the load and could change it without penalty.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Seasonal or deadline work can pile hours onto everyone involved.
A newborn, an ill relative or a house move can fill every hour of a home with no one's wish behind it.
Poor planning can produce relentless demands without anyone noticing the cumulative cost.
common_false_positives: A crisis-response week for emergency staff, followed by agreed recovery time.
A founder working punishing hours on their own venture by choice.
Parenting a baby, where broken sleep comes from the baby's needs and not from anyone's rules.
discernment_questions: Is there a date, or a clear condition, when this pace ends?
Is anyone else on the same schedule, including the person setting it?
When I say I'm too tired, is the toll acknowledged or does the pace stay as it was?
Have I noticed my ability to decide or object shrinking as my sleep has?
Do I get any hours that are mine?
less_concerning_if: The pace has an end date and that date is honored.
Rest is protected when you ask for it.
The people setting the pace live under it too.
more_concerning_if: Sleep or meals are directly controlled by others, such as being woken, kept up, or having food timed.
Exhaustion goes together with fear of what happens if you slow down: lost housing, pay or standing.
The schedule keeps you from friends and family, so nobody outside sees the state you are in.
pattern_over_time_signs: Rest days vanish one by one, and each loss is described as temporary.
You make more mistakes, and are then told the mistakes prove you need more structure.
Friends stop hearing from you because you have no hours left.
Small decisions you used to make, like when to eat or sleep, now wait for permission or do not happen.
Ritualized Exhaustion.repair_check: Look for rest that actually returns: a day off that stays off, a schedule that shortens, sleep that is left alone. A promise that things will calm down next month, repeated every month, is another pass of the same schedule.
Ritualized Exhaustion.boundary_respect_check: Ask for one protected block, such as a full night's sleep before a set hour, and see whether it holds on the third and fourth night as well as the first. A limit respected only when it costs nothing is easy to mistake for one that is kept.
Ritualized Exhaustion.psychological_mechanism: Long sleep loss and constant demand can reduce attention, memory and the ability to plan or weigh consequences. A tired person may take the nearest available option, accept requests they would otherwise refuse, and have little energy left to question the arrangement. The schedule can also use up the very time in which someone might talk to friends, look at alternatives or simply think.
Ritualized Exhaustion.possible_impact_on_receiver: Accounts include fog, irritability, getting sick more often, forgetting simple things, and a feeling of watching one's own life from a distance. Some lose the ability to picture an alternative, or the energy to want one. Others notice how quickly their thinking cleared after a few nights of real sleep.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask about the shape of the load rather than its fairness: 'How long do you expect this pace to last, and what could ease it?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Make one small request in plain terms: 'I do better work when I've slept. Could late-night requests wait until morning?'
response_options.disengagement: Protect small pockets of rest without announcing them or arguing about them: a short walk, a meal eaten sitting down, ten minutes of quiet.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a doctor about your sleep and workload, and a trusted friend or advocate about the schedule itself. If anyone controls when you may sleep or eat, an advocate can help you plan privately.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Write down hours worked and requests received, with dates. A manager, HR contact, union representative or employment advice service can compare them with your agreement or local rules.

Ritualized Exhaustion.boundary_script: "On this little sleep I can't think clearly, and I do want to do this well. Can we agree on which of these things really have to be done tonight, and which can wait until tomorrow?"
Ritualized Exhaustion.safety_note: Forced sleep loss and an unbroken schedule can sit alongside exploitative work or a group that rations rest. They can also be part of coercive control, a web of rules, checks and threats that runs your days. Watch for being woken or kept up by others, food or sleep used as reward, punishment for refusing, and shrinking contact with outsiders. A doctor, a labor-rights service or a domestic abuse advocate can help you plan privately, and keeping dated notes somewhere the other person cannot find them helps.
misuse_warning: Describing a busy season or a new baby as ritualized exhaustion mislabels ordinary strain and can sour a relationship over circumstances nobody chose.
Applying the label to an employer's heavy demands without looking at pay, agreement and end date can hide a simple contract dispute that has its own remedies.
Ritualized Exhaustion.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Resource Sabotage takes away the tools and support you need so that you fail, while ritualized exhaustion leaves the tools alone and fills your hours. "Managed Out" Through Exhaustion is a loss of purpose and belonging at work over months, so the person ends up sidelined rather than overloaded. Emotion Control works on what you may show, and this one works on how much you have left.

Spatial Invasion.short_definition: Standing too close, blocking a doorway or cornering someone during tension, so they feel physically hemmed in though nothing is threatened aloud.
Spatial Invasion.core_meaning: Standing too close, blocking a doorway or cornering someone during tension, so they feel physically hemmed in though nothing is threatened aloud.
Spatial Invasion.expanded_definition: Spatial invasion is the use of body position in a conflict: standing within arm's reach, stepping into a doorway, backing someone toward a wall, following from room to room. No spoken word needs to be threatening, which makes it hard to describe afterward. A crowded elevator or a cramped kitchen forces closeness on everyone. What marks the pattern is that the closeness or blocking appears when things get tense, narrows your way out, and returns each time. The body often reacts before the mind has a name for it.
Spatial Invasion.plain_language_summary: During an argument someone stands so close, or so squarely in your way, that you feel trapped, though they never say anything threatening.
Spatial Invasion.why_this_matters: The body reacts to a blocked exit well before there are words for it, so fear arrives in a conversation where nothing was ever threatened out loud.
what_it_is: Closing the distance during a disagreement until you are within arm's reach, or backed against furniture or a wall.
Standing in a doorway, hallway or beside a car door so the quickest way out is blocked.
Following you from room to room while the argument carries on.
Taking up the only path, step or seat so you cannot pass without touching or asking.
Leaving nothing quotable: the message sits in where a body is placed, which is why people doubt themselves afterward.
what_it_sounds_like: They step in as you stand to leave the room, and stay there while they keep talking.
You reach the hallway and find them already standing in it.
Their face is inches from yours while they speak quietly.
Where do you think you're going? We're not done.
You back up one step at a time until the wall is behind you.
They stand against the closed door of the room you are in.
Sit down. I'm talking to you.
what_it_is_not: Personal-space norms vary widely between cultures and individuals, and small rooms, elevators and crowded venues force closeness on everyone. A closeness noticed and corrected once is not this.
Leaning in to hear someone in a loud room.
A parent standing in a doorway to stop a toddler running toward the road.
Someone upset who stands near you and moves back as soon as you say it is too close.
Sharing a narrow hallway or kitchen where both of you shuffle past each other.
A person who steps nearer because they are hard of hearing or have low vision.
this_may_be_it_when: The closeness appears mainly in arguments and not in calm moments.
When you step away, they move with you to keep the gap closed or the exit covered.
You find yourself planning where to stand before a difficult talk, so as to stay near a door.
They stay close after you have said it feels too near.
Your body reacts (racing heart, shaking, going quiet) before anything has been said.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They step back when you ask for room.
The space is cramped and they are as squeezed as you are.
The same closeness shows up in warm moments, such as hugs.
You can walk out of the room freely and nobody follows.
They have asked whether this distance is okay.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Crowded buses, elevators and small apartments put people closer than anyone would choose.
People raised with closer conversational distance may stand nearer with no wish to unsettle you.
Someone hard of hearing or short-sighted may step in simply to follow what is said.
common_false_positives: A friend leaning in over the noise in a bar.
A relative who blocks a doorway while chatting and steps aside the moment you ask.
Someone standing in a hallway because a child, a pet or a hot pan is in the way.
discernment_questions: Does the closeness show up in tense moments and not in easy ones?
When I move, do they move with me?
Can I leave the room whenever I want and be let past without comment?
Does my body react before any words have been said?
When I say it is too close, does the distance change?
less_concerning_if: They step back as soon as you say you need room.
The same person stands equally near in relaxed moments.
The setting is cramped and the closeness is shared.
more_concerning_if: Blocking or following goes together with raised voices, slammed doors, or things thrown or broken nearby.
It moves on to holding, grabbing, or taking your keys or phone.
You have started avoiding rooms where you would be alone with them, or arranging your day around exits.
pattern_over_time_signs: You choose where to sit so you are never farthest from the door.
You avoid starting conversations in small rooms.
Your shoulders tighten when you hear them approach.
You stop raising issues at home, because raising them has meant being cornered.
Spatial Invasion.repair_check: Watch the physical record, not the words. After an apology, do they leave you the doorway, keep an arm's length and let you walk out of a room mid-sentence? Sorrow said while the same positioning returns in the next argument has changed nothing you can feel.
Spatial Invasion.boundary_respect_check: Notice whether a quiet request for more room changes where their body goes, not just what they say. Distance that opens and stays open is a request respected. Distance that closes again within the minute, or a response that mocks the request, is not.
Spatial Invasion.psychological_mechanism: Humans react to people very close to them and to blocked ways out without needing to think. Being cornered can set off a fight-or-flight response before any words register, which can leave the person afraid and then doubting the fear, because nothing was said. With no sentence to quote, the person may also struggle to explain it to others, which can add to the doubt.
Spatial Invasion.possible_impact_on_receiver: Accounts include a pounding heart, shaking, a dry mouth, and going quiet or freezing in the moment. Afterward there may be self-doubt, since nothing was said that could be repeated. Some start steering conversations toward open rooms, sitting near exits or avoiding being alone with the person, and the habit can stay in other settings long after.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for a small change in the setting: 'Can we both sit down for this? I find it easier to talk with a little room.'
response_options.firm_boundary: If it feels safe, say once and quietly: 'I need a bit more room to think.' If it does not feel safe, skip the words and focus on staying near a way out.
response_options.disengagement: If a talk starts to close in, move toward a shared space where others are present, or step out for water or the bathroom. The aim is distance without a confrontation.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell someone you trust what happens in your body in these moments, and ask a domestic abuse advocate how to plan for them. An advocate can talk through safety planning without you having to say anything to the other person.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, note dates, places and who was present, and report to a manager, HR or a union representative. Ask for meetings in open spaces or with a third person there.

Spatial Invasion.boundary_script: "I'd like us to sit down for this. I think better with a bit of space between us, and I want to hear what you're saying."
Spatial Invasion.safety_note: Blocked doors and cornering can come before, or sit beside, grabbing, threats, or taking keys and phones. Watch for blocking that grows more frequent, any holding or pushing, fear of being alone with them, or being unable to leave a room. A domestic abuse advocate can help you plan exits and what to keep within reach, and emergency services are for when you are being held or hurt right now.
misuse_warning: Reading any close or crowded moment as invasion can turn a cramped kitchen or a loud bar into an accusation. The label fits closeness that tightens in conflict and blocks your way.
Using the label for a person who stood in a doorway once while upset turns a worry about safety into a verdict. Look at repetition, and at what happens when you ask for room.
Spatial Invasion.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Nonverbal Dominance unsettles through looks, sighs and eye rolls and can work from across a room. Spatial invasion works through where a body stands, closing distance or covering the way out. Emotion Control penalizes the feelings you show and does not depend on where anyone stands. Resource Sabotage removes tools and support over weeks, while this plays out inside one tense moment.

Resource Sabotage.short_definition: Withdrawing the tools, information, money or help a person needs to do something, then treating the resulting failure as proof they are not up to it.
Resource Sabotage.core_meaning: Withdrawing the tools, information, money or help a person needs to do something, then treating the resulting failure as proof they are not up to it.
Resource Sabotage.expanded_definition: Resource sabotage is a pattern in which what someone needs to succeed goes missing: the budget is cut, the login stops working, the car is unavailable, the instructions never get passed on. The shortfall is then treated as the person's own failing. It can occur in a job, a household, a study program or a caring role. Shortages happen to everyone. Look at whether the gap lands on one person, tends to arrive just before something important, and goes unmentioned when the work then falls short.
Resource Sabotage.plain_language_summary: The things you need to succeed keep going missing, and then the failure is blamed on you.
Resource Sabotage.why_this_matters: Failing without the tools needed to succeed reads to everyone watching, and often to the person themselves, as plain incompetence.
what_it_is: Information that never reaches you, such as a changed deadline, a moved meeting or a form you were meant to see.
Access cut off at the point it matters: a shared login, a car, a key, a bank card, a budget line.
Help promised and then withdrawn at the last minute, such as childcare or a handover.
Followed by blame: the missed target is described as your lack of drive or skill, with no mention of what was missing.
Shows up in workplaces, households with shared money or transport, studies and creative projects.
what_it_sounds_like: Oh, I thought I told you the venue had changed.
The budget got reallocated. Surely you can still make it work.
I can't drive you, I have my own things. But you knew the exam was today.
If you were more organized you'd have found the file yourself.
Funny, everyone else got the memo.
You should have asked for the login sooner. (It was changed without notice.)
The one piece of equipment you need goes to someone else the week before your presentation.
what_it_is_not: Budgets get cut, colleagues forget things, and money and attention are legitimately redirected for real, stated reasons. The question is whether the shortfall lands on everyone or only ever on one person, and whether the missing support is acknowledged when the work then fails.
A team-wide shortage that everyone is working around together.
An honest mistake, such as an email sent to the wrong list, put right quickly once pointed out.
A partner who truly cannot help this week because of their own crisis, and says so.
A manager who turns down a request for a reason given openly and suggests an alternative.
A spending limit agreed jointly in a family budget.
this_may_be_it_when: The missing item is missing for you and not for people in similar positions.
Support disappears close to a deadline, exam, interview or launch.
Requests for the missing item meet delays or a shifting set of reasons.
When the work falls short, nobody mentions the missing support.
The thing withdrawn was previously available to you.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Everyone in your position faces the same shortfall.
The reason was given before the gap mattered.
Once you raise it, the item or an alternative arrives.
The person who withdrew it also bears the cost and says so.
It happened once, and the person took responsibility for the knock-on effect.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Organizations cut budgets and lose staff for reasons that have nothing to do with any one employee.
People forget a message or a ride when overloaded.
Households sometimes pull back money or time when they are under real strain.
common_false_positives: A shared project where everyone received the same late brief.
A teacher or boss who holds back hints so you can learn to solve it yourself, has said so, and checks in.
A funding shortage that halts several programs at once.
discernment_questions: Does the shortfall affect others in my position, or only me?
When I raise a missing item, is it restored, or do new obstacles appear?
Does what is missing keep arriving just before something important?
When the work falls short, is the missing support part of the account?
Could I show a neutral colleague or friend a list of what went missing and when?
less_concerning_if: The shortage is shared and its cause is stated openly.
Missing items are restored quickly once you flag them.
The person acknowledges the knock-on effect when your work suffers.
more_concerning_if: What goes missing is money, transport or documents, or the tools for work or study, and you rely on them.
Your failure is cited in front of others, in reviews or family talk, with the gap left out.
Access is cut right after you did well, sought independence or voiced a disagreement.
pattern_over_time_signs: A growing list of things that used to be yours to use are now held by someone else.
You start double-checking, backing up, and carrying your own copies of everything.
Your record of failures grows, though your skill has not changed.
You ask less often, since asking has produced delay or a new reason.
Resource Sabotage.repair_check: Check whether the missing thing is back in your hands with no strings attached, and whether the next shortfall is named at the time rather than discovered later. A heartfelt apology while access stays withheld has restored nothing you can use.
Resource Sabotage.boundary_respect_check: Ask in plain terms for the one item you need by a stated day, and see whether it appears on that day. If it arrives with no commentary on how you asked, the request was respected. If new conditions or reasons attach, the shortfall is still operating.
Resource Sabotage.psychological_mechanism: When the tools for a task go missing, the person who fails is usually the only one anyone looks at, and the missing support can be forgotten by everyone, including them. Repeated failures can wear down confidence and lead the person to ask for less, depend more, and accept the story that the problem is them. Control over money, transport or information also raises the cost of objecting.
Resource Sabotage.possible_impact_on_receiver: Common accounts: working harder and getting less, always feeling slightly behind, and shame about failures that cannot be fully explained. Some begin keeping copies, receipts and lists to show what went missing. Others stop applying for things or asking for help, since asking brought delay. Seeing the whole list written out can bring relief.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask what you need and when: 'The file I need for Thursday hasn't arrived. Can you tell me when I'll get it?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Put the request in writing, with a date, and keep a copy: 'I need the login and the budget figures by Wednesday to finish on time.'
response_options.disengagement: Build your own backup: copies of key files, a second route to your work, a little money or a ride you control. That reduces how much one withheld item can stop you.
response_options.support_seeking: Show a list of what went missing, and when, to a friend, mentor or advocate who can compare it with what others had. If money or housing depends on the person, legal aid can look at your options privately.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Keep a dated log of requests and responses, follow up by email, and raise the pattern with a manager, HR or a union representative along with its effect on your results.

Resource Sabotage.boundary_script: "I can only do this well if I have the figures and the login. Could you tell me today when I'll have them, so I can plan around it?"
Resource Sabotage.safety_note: Cut-off money, transport, documents or phones can be part of financial or coercive control, meaning control kept up through dependence and fear, especially at home. Watch for needing permission to spend, being kept from your own accounts or papers, or fear of what happens if you ask. A financial abuse advocate or legal aid service can help you plan, and copies of important documents are safest with someone you trust.
misuse_warning: Calling every shortage or forgotten message sabotage turns ordinary mistakes into accusations. The label fits a gap that falls on one person, repeatedly, and is then blamed on them.
Raising it at work without dates or comparisons can sound like blame when what you hold is a timeline worth showing.
Resource Sabotage.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Ritualized Exhaustion fills your hours so you have nothing left, while resource sabotage takes away what you need for the task itself. "Managed Out" Through Exhaustion is a slow thinning of purpose and visibility across months, whereas this concerns particular tasks and the tools for them. Nonverbal Dominance unsettles you in a moment with looks, and takes no tools away.

\"Managed Out\" Through Exhaustion.short_definition: Slowly removing a person's meaningful work, visibility and belonging until their departure looks like a free choice on paper.
\"Managed Out\" Through Exhaustion.core_meaning: Slowly removing a person's meaningful work, visibility and belonging until their departure looks like a free choice on paper.
\"Managed Out\" Through Exhaustion.expanded_definition: Being managed out is a gradual loss of a place: projects are reassigned, invitations to meetings stop, feedback dries up, and the person is left with little to do and no one asking for their view. Nothing is formally taken away and no complaint is filed, so a resignation reads as their own decision. Restructures and role changes hollow out jobs too. Telling signs are a loss that is quiet, falls on one person, and often starts after a conflict, a complaint or a change of leadership.
\"Managed Out\" Through Exhaustion.plain_language_summary: Your work, your say and your place at the table slip away bit by bit, until quitting starts to feel like your only choice.
\"Managed Out\" Through Exhaustion.why_this_matters: A departure produced by these conditions looks, on paper and in memory, like a free choice, which leaves the person carrying the story that they simply could not cope.
what_it_is: Meaningful projects reassigned one at a time, with no conversation.
Being dropped from meetings, email threads and decisions you used to take part in.
Praise and feedback stop, and reviews turn vague or oddly critical.
No formal step is ever taken, so there is nothing to appeal or complain about.
Mainly seen at work, and also in volunteer groups, congregations and family businesses.
what_it_sounds_like: We're just going in a different direction.
Don't worry about that meeting. It wouldn't be useful for you.
You're welcome to stay, of course. Nobody is pushing you.
We thought you had enough on your plate. (As the project goes to someone else.)
Your calendar goes from full to nearly empty over a few months.
You hear about a decision in your own team from a colleague, after the fact.
Maybe it's time to think about what you really want.
what_it_is_not: Restructures, shrinking budgets and real role mismatches hollow out jobs, and an employer in decline has less for everyone. A transparent change across a group differs from a quiet removal that falls on one person while no complaint is filed.
A skills mismatch discussed openly, with a plan to move you or train you.
A planned handover to a successor, announced and explained.
A documented performance process with stated expectations and a chance to meet them. It can be painful and still be transparent.
Seasonal quiet in a role where work comes in waves.
this_may_be_it_when: The reduction affects you and not colleagues with similar roles.
It began soon after you raised a complaint, disagreed, or took leave.
Nobody will tell you what has changed or why, and requests for a conversation get put off.
Your responsibilities shrink while your title and pay stay the same.
People are friendly, but nothing you do brings the work back.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The change was announced, explained, and applies to a group.
Someone has offered a path: a new project, training or a move.
Your workload dropped when a project ended, and new work is being planned.
A formal process exists and you have been told what is expected.
Colleagues in your role describe the same thinning.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Teams reorganize and priorities shift without any one person in mind.
A busy manager may stop including someone through habit and oversight.
A person's skills and the role can drift apart, and a quiet period follows.
common_false_positives: A slow season in a project-driven job.
Being moved off a project after a clear change in company strategy.
A new manager taking time to learn who does what.
discernment_questions: Is the change announced and shared, or silent and limited to me?
Has anyone given me a reason, a plan or a date?
Did the change follow a particular event, such as a complaint or a disagreement?
Are colleagues in similar roles going through the same thing?
If I did go, would it look like a free choice on paper?
less_concerning_if: The change is explained and applies across a team.
A conversation about your role is available and leads somewhere.
New work or training appears when you ask.
more_concerning_if: You are told it is up to you whether to stay while the conditions keep worsening.
Your pay, visa, health cover or housing is tied to the job.
Records of the change are missing, so nothing shows what happened.
pattern_over_time_signs: Month by month, your calendar and inbox thin out.
People who used to ask for your view stop asking.
A mention of your performance appears in conversation without any earlier feedback.
You begin to question whether you ever did good work.
\"Managed Out\" Through Exhaustion.repair_check: Look for work and a voice actually restored: a real project with real decisions attached, a seat back at meetings, a straight conversation about what happened. Reassurance that you are valued, while the calendar stays empty, has repaired nothing.
\"Managed Out\" Through Exhaustion.boundary_respect_check: Ask in writing for a conversation about your role and what is expected. Watch whether a date is set and kept, and whether what you hear matches what happens next. Being told nothing has changed, while the empty calendar says otherwise, answers a different question.
\"Managed Out\" Through Exhaustion.psychological_mechanism: Work gives people purpose, status and routine, and losing them gradually can feel more like personal inadequacy than like something happening to them. Because nothing is formally removed, there is no event to point to, which can make the person doubt their own read. As confidence falls, going can start to look like relief, and the departure may be recorded and remembered as a free choice.
\"Managed Out\" Through Exhaustion.possible_impact_on_receiver: Accounts include dread on Sunday evenings, checking whether you have been left off an email, feeling invisible, and doubting your own competence. Some wonder whether they imagined the change. Afterward, some carry the belief that they could not cope even when they did their work well, while others feel relief on seeing it laid out.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask a plain question about the work: 'I've noticed I'm not on the planning meetings anymore. Is that a change in my role?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Request clarity in writing: 'Could we meet this week to talk about my responsibilities and what is expected of me over the next quarter?'
response_options.disengagement: Put quiet energy into skills, contacts and records outside the situation, and decide privately what you want before taking any step.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk to a trusted colleague outside your chain, a mentor or a counselor about what you are seeing. An employment advice service or union can explain your rights before you decide anything.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Keep a dated log of projects removed, meetings dropped and feedback received, and keep your own reviews and praise where company policy allows. Raise the pattern with HR or a union representative.

\"Managed Out\" Through Exhaustion.boundary_script: "Help me understand how my role has changed over the last few months. Could we set up a time to talk about what I'm responsible for and what you expect from me?"
\"Managed Out\" Through Exhaustion.safety_note: This is chiefly a threat to income and standing, though a visa or housing tied to the job raises the stakes. Concern grows if pay or immigration status depends on staying, if you are pressed to sign a separation agreement quickly, or if the strain is hurting your sleep or health. Get advice from an employment lawyer, union or legal aid service before signing, and keep dated notes of what changed.
misuse_warning: Reading every quiet spell or reassignment as being managed out can turn ordinary reorganizing into a grievance. The label needs a comparison, a timeline and a lack of explanation, not just a bad feeling.
Telling a coworker they are being managed out can add to their distress or push a decision that the evidence does not support.
\"Managed Out\" Through Exhaustion.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Resource Sabotage takes away tools and information for a task and cites the failure, while being managed out takes away the role itself, across months, with no task to fail at. Ritualized Exhaustion overloads you until nothing is left, the opposite of the empty calendar here. Emotion Control sets which feelings may show and has nothing to do with the work you are given.

Evidence Traps.short_definition: Saving a person's messages, posts or remarks without their context, then bringing them out later at a moment when they do the most damage.
Evidence Traps.core_meaning: Saving a person's messages, posts or remarks without their context, then bringing them out later at a moment when they do the most damage.
Evidence Traps.expanded_definition: Evidence traps are genuine words, screenshots or recordings that are kept rather than answered, then returned later with the surrounding conversation removed. Nothing is faked, which is why it is hard to dispute. A joke becomes a position, and a vent at midnight becomes a confession. Keeping records is ordinary and often wise, and people do bring up old remarks. What stands out is comments stored instead of discussed at the time, context stripped away, and a return that arrives in a moment of conflict, review or dispute.
Evidence Traps.plain_language_summary: Things you said casually are saved, then held up later without their context, so that everything you say starts to feel like it could be used against you.
Evidence Traps.why_this_matters: Knowing that anything said may be stored and re-timed makes ordinary candor feel risky, and speech starts being drafted rather than spoken.
what_it_is: Real material, such as texts, posts, voice notes and emails, that is kept and later quoted in part.
The original exchange often had a tone, a joke or an earlier message that has been left out.
It surfaces at a chosen point: an argument, a performance review, a group dispute, a custody or legal exchange.
Different from forgery: the words are yours, and the harm lies in what is cut away and when it appears.
Occurs in relationships, friendships, families, workplaces and online communities.
what_it_sounds_like: Oh, you don't remember saying this? I have it right here.
Here's what you wrote in March. So you did say you hated your job.
I've been keeping this for a while.
A screenshot cropped to show only your angriest line, posted to a group chat.
You said it, so don't tell me you didn't mean it.
A colleague pastes one line of your email into a meeting thread without the lines around it.
I took a screenshot back then, just in case.
what_it_is_not: Keeping records is legitimate and often wise, and raising something someone said because it still matters, in the context it was said in, is just conversation. What is being described is the stripping of that context and the choosing of the moment it returns.
Quoting an email in a work dispute with the full thread attached.
Saving threatening or abusive messages to show an advocate, lawyer or police. That is documentation for safety, a different use altogether.
A friend who remembers what you said and says 'but you told me last week' in good faith.
Receipts kept for an HR or legal process and shared in full with the people entitled to see them.
this_may_be_it_when: Something said weeks ago, which got no reply then, comes back in the middle of an unrelated argument.
Only the sharpest line returns, without the lines before or after it.
Other people are shown the quote before you are told it is being raised.
A casual remark is treated as a formal commitment or confession.
You find out items were saved at the time and not simply remembered.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The quote comes with the surrounding exchange and you are free to explain it.
It is raised promptly and plainly, as in 'this bothered me when you said it'.
The record is being kept to document threats or abuse.
They are equally open about their own messages being shared back.
You asked for the thing to be kept, such as a promise put in writing.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People often keep chats and emails for practical reasons, and referring back is a normal way to settle a factual question.
Memory itself can bring up an old remark in a heated moment, with nothing stored.
Cloud backups and message history keep things automatically, with no plan behind it.
common_false_positives: A boss who keeps an email thread confirming what was agreed.
A partner who quotes your promise of a deadline in full, since it was a plan you both made.
An app's 'on this day' memory resurfacing an old post.
discernment_questions: Does the quote still mean the same thing once the surrounding messages are put back?
Was it ever raised at the time, or only now?
Is it being used to settle a question, or to quiet me?
Do I now draft my words with an audience in mind?
Would they be willing to show the full thread to a third person we both respect?
less_concerning_if: Old messages are quoted in full and with context, and you are free to explain.
Records are kept in the open and you can keep copies too.
Concerns are raised promptly rather than banked.
more_concerning_if: Stored material comes with threats to share it with family, an employer or a court.
Recordings are made without your knowledge during emotional moments.
Material is shared with others to shape their view of you before you can reply.
pattern_over_time_signs: You edit what you write, or stop confiding in writing at all.
More of your talk moves to calls or in person, where nothing is kept.
You are surprised by what has been kept: dates, screenshots, details.
Old remarks come back at each new dispute, whatever the subject.
Evidence Traps.repair_check: Repair would mean saying openly what was kept, showing the whole exchange, and raising concerns on the day they arise from now on. An apology that arrives while the folder of screenshots stays and keeps being used has changed nothing about how safe it is to speak.
Evidence Traps.boundary_respect_check: Ask that concerns be raised when they happen, not stored. Then see whether next month brings 'this bothered me', said that day, or another old quote out of nowhere. Also watch whether your own words are given the same openness.
Evidence Traps.psychological_mechanism: People relax their guard when they believe words fade, and talk more honestly as a result. Learning that remarks may be saved and replayed can make speech feel risky, so the person edits themselves, guards what they write, and may start to doubt their own earlier words when shown a fragment. Because the material is real, it is also hard to contest, which can add to the sense of being trapped.
Evidence Traps.possible_impact_on_receiver: Accounts include going quiet in writing, rereading messages before sending, feeling watched in your own home or friend group, and wariness about telling anyone anything. Doubt about what you really meant can set in when you are shown a fragment. Others feel anger that something said in trust was held back for later.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for the whole picture: 'Can you show me the messages around that one? I remember the conversation going differently.'
response_options.firm_boundary: If it feels safe, ask for concerns in real time: 'If something I say bothers you, tell me then, so we can sort it out together.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop sharing delicate things with someone who keeps them for later, and move sensitive talk to a call or an in-person conversation.
response_options.support_seeking: Show the full thread to someone neutral and ask how it reads. If material is being shared, or threatened to be, keep your own copies of what was sent and talk to an advocate or lawyer.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, keep your own copy of the full email thread, reply with the missing context in writing, and ask a manager or HR to review the whole exchange and not the fragment.

Evidence Traps.boundary_script: "I'm happy to talk about anything I've said, if we look at the whole conversation and talk about it when it comes up. I'd rather not have old messages brought out in the middle of something else."
Evidence Traps.safety_note: Someone quietly saving your words is pressure on trust, not a physical danger. The picture changes if saved material is paired with threats to release it, intimate images or recordings, a custody or legal case, or demands that you do something or stay. Keep your own copies of what has been sent, and take them to a lawyer or a domestic abuse or cyber-abuse advocate before replying to any threat.
misuse_warning: Calling any reminder of an earlier statement an evidence trap can make accountability look like an attack. People are entitled to say 'you told me this'.
Using the label to avoid being quoted accurately confuses stripped context with unwelcome content.
Evidence Traps.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Emotion Control penalizes a feeling as soon as it is shown, whereas evidence traps bank the remark and bring it out weeks later. Resource Sabotage takes away something you need in the present, and here the material is something you already gave. Unlike a faked screenshot, nothing in an evidence trap is invented; the words are yours.

Moral Framing.short_definition: Answering someone's boundary, objection or criticism with a judgment of their character, such as selfish or disloyal, instead of with the thing they raised.
Moral Framing.core_meaning: Answering someone's boundary, objection or criticism with a judgment of their character, such as selfish or disloyal, instead of with the thing they raised.
Moral Framing.expanded_definition: In moral framing, a boundary or complaint is met with a verdict on the kind of person who made it. A no becomes selfish, a fair criticism becomes disloyalty, a request for change becomes cruelty. The original issue drops out of sight, because the conversation is now about the person's worth. A hurt remark in a heated moment is common. The tell is character judgments replacing the subject every time, so a request has to be defended as virtue before it can be discussed.
Moral Framing.plain_language_summary: You say what you need or what bothered you, and the reply is about what kind of person you are, so the issue never gets discussed.
Moral Framing.why_this_matters: Once the subject has become what kind of person you are, the original issue is no longer on the table and cannot be settled.
what_it_is: Naming a moral failing, such as selfish, cold, ungrateful, disloyal or a bad mother, in reply to a specific request.
A reply that moves from the event to the person, so the question 'can we change this?' is never reached.
Often borrows values the person holds dear, such as family loyalty, generosity or faith, and turns them into a test.
Makes saying no feel like a character flaw instead of a choice.
Occurs in families, couples, friendships, congregations and workplaces.
what_it_sounds_like: A good daughter would come.
That's a really selfish way to think about this.
I never thought you'd be so cold.
After all we've done for you, this is how you repay us?
Decent people don't keep score.
If you cared about this family, you wouldn't be asking.
I'm disappointed in the person you've become.
what_it_is_not: Sometimes an observation about character is accurate, specific and offered as real feedback, and sometimes two people hold different values and read the same event through them. A hurt remark later walked back and replaced with substance is not this.
A specific, honest observation about a behavior, given along with a discussion of the issue itself.
A disagreement rooted in different values, such as how much to give to family, where each side explains their own.
Someone telling you honestly that your action conflicted with a promise you made.
A friend saying 'that wasn't like you' about something out of character, and asking what was going on.
this_may_be_it_when: Every boundary you set is answered with a character label.
The label is about you as a whole, such as 'selfish', and not about the single act.
You end up justifying your goodness instead of your request.
Your original point gets lost and is not addressed later.
Other people hear what kind of person you are, in terms like these, before you have spoken.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They address your request and add how they feel about it.
They describe the effect on them without labeling you.
They apologize for a harsh word and return to the topic.
Their values clearly differ and they say so without condemning yours.
The comment is specific to one act and accurate, and you would agree on reflection.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People often reach for moral language when hurt, because it is the language they learned for strong feeling.
Two people with different upbringings can read the same act as generosity or as a failure of duty.
Family or community expectations may be voiced as duty by someone repeating what was said to them.
common_false_positives: A friend saying 'that wasn't kind' about a comment you made, and explaining why.
A mentor giving accurate, difficult feedback about honesty in your work.
A family member expressing disappointment in a decision while still accepting it.
discernment_questions: After I state my need, is the next thing said about my request or about me?
Can the original issue be discussed once the label is set aside?
Do I find myself proving I am a good person instead of explaining what I need?
Does the person apply the same standards to themselves?
Is the character comment specific and accurate, or global and sweeping?
less_concerning_if: The sharp word is taken back and the topic resumes.
The label describes one act, not who you are.
Different values are stated as differences rather than as failings.
more_concerning_if: Other people are recruited to repeat the verdict.
Support, affection or belonging is offered only if you drop the boundary.
You begin to hold the label yourself and apologize for having needs.
pattern_over_time_signs: You say 'sorry, I know I'm being selfish' before asking for anything.
You stop making requests you would once have thought ordinary.
You weigh each choice by what it will say about you instead of by what you need.
Your sense of being a good person starts to depend on going along.
Moral Framing.repair_check: Watch whether the original topic gets its turn. If, after the character remark is withdrawn, the conversation returns to your request and the answer can be no without a new verdict, something has shifted. A kind apology that leaves the request unheard, and reappears next time, has not.
Moral Framing.boundary_respect_check: State the boundary once without defending your character, and see what is said next. If the reply is about the boundary, even in disagreement, it was heard. If the next thing you hear is a statement about who you are, the boundary became a test of your character.
Moral Framing.psychological_mechanism: Most people want to see themselves as good, and moral labels reach that wish directly. When a request is recast as a flaw, the person may drop the request to protect their self-image, because defending their character feels more urgent than the original point. If the language borrows values they hold, such as loyalty or generosity, giving in may seem consistent with who they believe they are.
Moral Framing.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe guilt out of proportion to what they asked for, rehearsing justifications, and apologizing for ordinary needs. Some say they started to doubt whether they were selfish, and gave in to prove otherwise. Others describe a mix of relief and anger on realizing that the question they raised was never answered.

response_options.soft_clarification: Bring the conversation back to the request: 'I hear that you think I'm being selfish. Can we go back to what I asked?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to argue character: 'I'm not going to debate whether I'm a good person. I've told you what I can do, and that is my answer.'
response_options.disengagement: If the labels keep coming, close the talk on the original topic: 'Let's leave this for now.' You do not need to win the point about who you are.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe the exact words used and your request to someone outside the situation, and ask whether the request seems reasonable. A counselor or a leader you trust can help separate your values from the pressure.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, restate the issue in neutral terms and in writing: 'To be clear, my request is about the schedule.' If personal remarks continue, note them and raise them with a manager or HR.

Moral Framing.boundary_script: "You may be right that we see this differently, but I'm asking about one specific thing. Can we talk about that request, and leave out what kind of person either of us is?"
Moral Framing.safety_note: Moral labels on their own press on your self-image, not on your physical safety. That can change when a judgment comes with threats of exposure to a community, loss of housing, money or contact with children or family, or being told you deserve harm. If a verdict carries that weight, speak to someone outside the group, such as an advocate, a counselor or legal aid, before deciding anything.
misuse_warning: Calling every disapproving remark moral framing can wave away honest feedback. Sometimes a hard thing is true and said kindly.
Using the label to dismiss a family's real worries about a decision you have made turns a pattern into a way to avoid a conversation.
Moral Framing.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Emotion Control penalizes certain feelings as they appear, while moral framing answers a boundary or complaint with a verdict on the person's goodness. Nonverbal Dominance conveys disapproval through sighs and stares without words, and this one is put into words. Resource Sabotage takes things away; here nothing is removed, and the request is simply turned into a test of your character.

Reproductive Coercion.short_definition: Pressuring or penalizing someone over whether, when or how to have children, through money, work, family standing or withdrawal of support.
Reproductive Coercion.core_meaning: Pressuring or penalizing someone over whether, when or how to have children, through money, work, family standing or withdrawal of support.
Reproductive Coercion.expanded_definition: Reproductive coercion is pressure over another person's decisions about pregnancy and children: whether to have a child, when, how many, whether to continue a pregnancy, or whether to use contraception. The pressure can come from a partner, relatives, an employer or an institution, and works through consequences: money, a job, housing, belonging or support made to depend on the answer. Stating hopes is normal. The line is crossed when a cost is attached to the answer and the pressure continues after it has been given.
Reproductive Coercion.plain_language_summary: Someone ties your job, money, home or place in the family to what you decide about having children, and keeps pressing after you have answered.
Reproductive Coercion.why_this_matters: A decision that belongs to one person's body and life ends up made under the weight of what refusal would cost them: job, money, support, standing in the family.
what_it_is: Consequences attached to a decision: pay, promotion, housing, money or support depend on having or not having a child.
Pressure repeated after you have given your answer, passed from partner to parents to in-laws to a community leader in turn.
Can include interference with contraception or with access to health care, which takes the decision out of your hands.
Can come from a partner, a family, an employer or an institution, and each works differently.
Runs in both directions: pressure to have a child, and pressure not to, or to end a pregnancy.
what_it_sounds_like: If you really loved me, you'd give me a baby.
People in this role who start families don't last here.
My parents will cut us off if there isn't a grandchild by next year.
We'll see how long your position lasts if you're expecting.
I'll support you only if you keep it. (Or: only if you end it.)
You don't get to decide that on your own.
You've said no three times, and we're not done talking.
what_it_is_not: People may want things and say so: a parent hoping for grandchildren, a partner describing the family they imagined. A neutral, lawful employment policy can touch a reproductive decision without targeting it. What changes the picture is a consequence attached to the answer.
A partner who says they want children, talks about timing, and accepts a 'no' or a 'not yet' while the relationship stays on the same terms.
Grandparents' hopes shared once or twice, with no money or standing attached.
A doctor or counselor explaining the medical risks of a pregnancy or a treatment, then leaving the decision to you.
Parental leave rules applied the same way to everyone at a workplace.
this_may_be_it_when: Money, housing or work is mentioned in the same breath as your decision.
The question is raised again right after you have answered it.
Other people are lined up to press you.
You have been told that your place in the family depends on it.
Your access to contraception, appointments or your own records has become something you must account for.
this_may_not_be_it_when: A wish is stated and then your answer is accepted.
Your income, home and standing do not change with your answer.
The pressure is one conversation and both sides are open.
Medical advice is given in full and the decision is left to you.
Everyone at the workplace is under the same stated policy.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People hope for grandchildren or a larger family, and say so without realizing how it weighs on you.
Couples often change their minds and need several conversations over years.
Employers have leave and scheduling rules that touch on parenthood without targeting any person.
common_false_positives: A relative asking 'any news?' at every holiday, who stops when told it is private.
A partner who is sad about a difference over children and grieves openly, with no leverage attached.
A clinic asking routine questions about pregnancy plans before prescribing.
discernment_questions: Is there a cost to me, in money, work, home or standing, tied to my answer?
Does the pressure stop when I answer, or does it come back?
Is anyone interfering with my contraception or appointments?
Can I say no, or not yet, and keep the same life?
Can I see a doctor on my own?
less_concerning_if: Hopes are voiced but your answer is accepted.
Support continues whichever way you decide.
Medical and practical information is shared openly, with the choice left to you.
more_concerning_if: Contraception, medication or appointments are controlled, hidden or monitored.
The pressure comes with threats about money, housing, children or immigration status.
Others in the family or workplace are being used to repeat the pressure.
pattern_over_time_signs: The question returns after each 'no', with higher stakes each time.
Your access to your own money, papers or health care has been shrinking.
You have started saying what is wanted to keep the peace.
Conversations about the future always lead back to children.
Reproductive Coercion.repair_check: Repair would mean the decision stays yours and the cost attached to it disappears: the support, the job conditions and the family welcome continue as before, whatever you decided. Regret expressed while the pressure or the conditions remain is not repair.
Reproductive Coercion.boundary_respect_check: After you have given an answer, notice whether the subject is closed or reopened. A respected answer is followed by an unchanged life and a different topic. If it is followed by a quiet drop in help, warmth or hours, or by a new person raising it, the answer is still being negotiated.
Reproductive Coercion.psychological_mechanism: When the price of a choice is housing, income or family belonging, the choice gets weighed against security instead of against one's own wishes. Pressure repeated through several people can make a 'no' feel selfish or impossible to hold, and reduced access to money or care can make going along seem the only workable route. Over time a person may report agreeing without feeling the decision was theirs.
Reproductive Coercion.possible_impact_on_receiver: Accounts include a sense that your body and future are being decided by others, dread around conversations about family, and anxiety about money or work. Some feel grief over a decision made under pressure, or anger years afterward. Others fear that questions about their health care would be followed by consequences.

response_options.soft_clarification: If it feels safe, answer briefly and without arguing: 'That's something I'm still thinking about. I'll let you know.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Ask for the topic to be set aside: 'I'd like to leave this for now, and I'd like to talk about something else.'
response_options.disengagement: Without announcing anything, keep your own medical appointments, records and money where you can reach them, and let a clinic know if you need to speak to a clinician alone.
response_options.support_seeking: A sexual and reproductive health clinic, a doctor or a domestic abuse advocate can talk with you privately. They can explain your options and how to keep care confidential where you live.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a work decision seems tied to pregnancy or plans for children, write down what was said and when, and take it to HR, a union representative or an employment-rights service before replying to anything.

Reproductive Coercion.boundary_script: "I understand this matters a lot to you. It's a decision about my own body and life, and I need to think it through at my own pace. Can we talk about something else for now?"
Reproductive Coercion.safety_note: Pressure about pregnancy can sit alongside violence, threats to money, housing, children or immigration status, and coercive control, a steady pattern of rules and threats that narrows your choices. Pregnancy can also be a time when abuse begins or worsens. Warning signs include controlled contraception or appointments, being watched at clinics, and threats tied to your answer. A domestic abuse hotline or clinic can talk privately; ask about safe ways to reach them from a phone or device the other person cannot see.
misuse_warning: Treating any wish for a child, or any employer's parental-leave policy, as coercion can silence honest wishes. The label fits consequences attached to the answer, not the wish.
Calling a partner's grief over a difference about children coercion can turn a painful, honest disagreement into an accusation.
Reproductive Coercion.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Resource Sabotage removes tools or support so that a task fails, while reproductive coercion ties the loss of money, work or support to a decision about children. "Managed Out" Through Exhaustion strips a person's place at work gradually, whereas here the consequence is tied to one decision and follows the answer. Emotion Control penalizes feelings generally, not a specific choice about family.
